Answer: 01
LLM & Transformer Fundamentals
Every GenAI interview starts here. Interviewers use these questions to check whether you understand
what's actually happening inside the model you're building products around — not just which API to call.
Q. Explain the Transformer architecture and why it replaced
RNNs for language modeling.
The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) processes an entire sequence in parallel using self-
attention, instead of stepping through tokens one at a time like an RNN or LSTM. Each token's
representation is updated by attending to every other token in the sequence, weighted by learned
relevance scores.
This solves two core RNN problems: (1) vanishing gradients over long sequences, since attention
gives every token a direct path to every other token regardless of distance, and (2) sequential
computation, since RNNs can't be parallelized across time steps during training, while
Transformers can process a whole batch of tokens simultaneously on a GPU.
A Transformer block = Multi-Head Self-Attention → Add & LayerNorm → Feed-Forward Network →
Add & LayerNorm, stacked N times. Positional encodings are added at the input because attention
itself is order-agnostic.
Interview tip — If asked to draw it, sketch: Input Embeddings + Positional Encoding → [Self-
Attention → Add&Norm → FFN → Add&Norm] × N → Output.
FOUNDATIONAL
Q. Walk through self-attention mathematically. What are Q,
K, and V?
Each token embedding is projected into three vectors using learned weight matrices: Query (Q),
Key (K), and Value (V). Intuitively, Q represents 'what this token is looking for,' K represents 'what
this token offers,' and V is 'the actual content it contributes.'
Attention scores are computed as the scaled dot product of Q and K: softmax(Query times Key-transpose / square root of d-k) V.
The scaling by square root of d-k prevents the dot products from growing too large in magnitude as
dimensionality increases, which would push softmax into regions with vanishing gradients.
Multi-head attention runs this process h times in parallel with different learned projections, letting
the model attend to different types of relationships (syntax, coreference, long-range dependency)
simultaneously, then concatenates and projects the results back down.
FOUNDATIONAL

Answer: Q. What is the difference between encoder-only, decoder-
only, and encoder-decoder architectures?
Encoder-only (BERT-style): bidirectional attention — every token attends to every other token,
including future ones. Best for understanding tasks: classification, embeddings, NER.
Decoder-only (GPT, LLaMA, Claude-style): causal (masked) attention — each token can only attend
to previous tokens. This autoregressive property is what enables text generation one token at a
time. Nearly all modern production LLMs are decoder-only because it scales well and unifies
pretraining with generation.
Encoder-decoder (T5, original Transformer, BART): the encoder builds a bidirectional
representation of the input, and the decoder cross-attends to it while generating output
autoregressively. Well suited to sequence-to-sequence tasks like translation and summarization
where input and output are distinct sequences.
FOUNDATIONAL
Q. What is next-token prediction, and why is a simple
objective enough to produce reasoning-like behavior?
Pretraining minimizes cross-entropy loss between the predicted probability distribution over the
vocabulary and the actual next token, across trillions of tokens of text. It is a single, simple, self-
supervised objective — no labels required.
Reasoning-like behavior emerges because predicting the next token well on diverse, high-quality
text implicitly requires learning grammar, facts, world knowledge, and multi-step logical patterns
— the model can't compress that much text accurately without internalizing structure. This is
often called emergent capability: certain skills (arithmetic, chain-of-thought, code generation)
appear abruptly once model and data scale pass a threshold, rather than improving smoothly.
INTERMEDIATE
Q. Explain KV caching and why it matters for inference
latency and cost.
During autoregressive generation, computing attention for a new token requires the Key and
Value vectors of every previous token. Without caching, you'd recompute K and V for the entire
prefix at every single generation step — O(n squared) redundant work over a sequence of length n.
KV caching stores the K and V tensors for all previously processed tokens in GPU memory, so each
new token only needs one forward pass through the model, reusing cached K/V instead of
recomputing them. This turns generation from quadratic into roughly linear cost per step.
The tradeoff is memory: KV cache size grows with sequence length × batch size × number of
layers × hidden size, and it's frequently the actual bottleneck limiting how many concurrent
requests a GPU can serve — which is why techniques like PagedAttention (vLLM), multi-query
attention (MQA), and grouped-query attention (GQA) exist.
Interview tip — GQA is a favorite follow-up: it shares K/V heads across groups of query heads,
cutting KV cache size with minimal quality loss — used in LLaMA 2/3, Mistral.
INTERMEDIATE

Answer: Q. What is the difference between pretraining, supervised
fine-tuning (SFT), and RLHF/preference tuning?
Pretraining: next-token prediction on massive unlabeled text corpora. This is where the model
acquires language ability and world knowledge — it is by far the most compute-intensive stage.
SFT (instruction tuning): fine-tuning on curated (prompt, ideal response) pairs so the base model
learns to follow instructions and adopt a helpful assistant format, rather than just continuing text
in a document-completion style.
RLHF / DPO (preference tuning): the model's outputs are ranked by humans (or a reward model
trained on human preferences), and the policy is optimized to produce outputs humans prefer —
improving helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness beyond what SFT alone achieves. DPO (Direct
Preference Optimization) achieves a similar effect without training a separate reward model or
running RL, directly optimizing the policy on preference pairs, which is simpler and more stable to
train.
INTERMEDIATE
Q. What is temperature, top-k, and top-p (nucleus)
sampling? How do they differ?
Temperature reshapes the probability distribution before sampling: dividing logits by T < 1
sharpens the distribution (more deterministic, favors high-probability tokens), while T > 1 flattens
it (more random/creative). T = 0 is effectively greedy decoding.
Top-k sampling restricts sampling to only the k highest-probability tokens, discarding the long tail
entirely — a fixed cutoff regardless of how the probability mass is distributed.
Top-p (nucleus) sampling instead selects the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability
exceeds p (e.g., 0.9), so the candidate pool adapts dynamically — narrow when the model is
confident, wider when it's uncertain. In practice, top-p is generally preferred over top-k for this
adaptiveness, and both are often combined with temperature.
FOUNDATIONAL
Q. What are the main scaling laws for LLMs, and what did
Chinchilla change about them?
Kaplan et al. (2020) showed loss decreases predictably as a power law with model size, dataset
size, and compute — and, given a compute budget, argued for prioritizing larger models over
more data, which drove the era of very large but undertrained models like GPT-3.
Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022) re-ran the analysis more rigorously and found that most models
of that era were significantly undertrained relative to their size — for a fixed compute budget,
model size and training tokens should scale roughly equally (roughly ~20 tokens per parameter is
the commonly cited rule of thumb). This is why later model families (LLaMA, etc.) trained smaller
models on far more tokens and got better performance per FLOP.
ADVANCED

Answer: Q. What is the difference between quantization approaches
like INT8, INT4, GPTQ, and AWQ?
Quantization reduces the numerical precision of model weights (and sometimes activations) from
FP16/BF16 down to INT8 or INT4, shrinking memory footprint and increasing throughput, at some
cost to output quality.
Post-training quantization (PTQ) methods like GPTQ minimize the layer-wise reconstruction error
by solving a per-layer optimization problem after training, without needing to retrain — it's
popular for INT4 quantization with minimal accuracy loss.
AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) observes that not all weights are equally important
— it identifies and preserves precision for the small fraction of weight channels that correspond to
high-magnitude activations, since those matter disproportionately for output quality, and
quantizes the rest more aggressively.
In interviews, the practical framing matters most: quantization is usually the first lever engineers
pull to fit a model on smaller/cheaper GPUs or increase batch throughput, and the trade is
memory/speed vs. a measurable (though often small) quality regression that should be evaluated
on your actual task, not just perplexity.
ADVANCED
Q. What is positional encoding, and how do RoPE and ALiBi
differ from the original sinusoidal approach?
Self-attention has no inherent notion of token order — it treats a sequence like an unordered set
unless position information is explicitly injected. The original Transformer added fixed sinusoidal
position vectors directly to token embeddings before the first layer.
RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) instead encodes position by rotating the Query and Key vectors
by an angle proportional to their position, applied at every attention layer rather than only at the
input. This gives it a useful property: the attention score between two tokens depends naturally on
their relative distance, and it extrapolates to longer sequences better than fixed sinusoidal
encodings. RoPE is used in LLaMA, Mistral, and most modern open-weight decoder-only models.
ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases) skips positional embeddings entirely and instead directly
biases attention scores by a penalty proportional to the distance between tokens — closer tokens
get less penalty. It's simpler and was designed specifically for strong length extrapolation (training
short, running long) with minimal extra compute.
ADVANCED

Answer: Q. What is Mixture of Experts (MoE), and why are labs
increasingly using it for frontier models?
MoE replaces a single dense feed-forward block in each Transformer layer with multiple 'expert'
feed-forward networks, plus a lightweight learned router that decides which few experts (e.g., 2 of
8) process each token. Only the selected experts' weights are activated for a given token, not the
full parameter set.
This decouples total parameter count from per-token compute cost: a model can have a very large
total parameter count (more capacity/knowledge) while the actual FLOPs spent per token stay
close to a much smaller dense model — you get the quality benefits of scale without paying the
full inference cost for every token.
The tradeoffs interviewers want to hear: routing can be unstable to train (load balancing losses
are needed so experts aren't over/under-used), MoE models need more total GPU memory to hold
all experts even though only a few are active per token, and serving them efficiently requires
careful expert-parallelism infrastructure — it's a systems-engineering problem as much as a
modeling one.

Prompt Engineering
Prompt engineering questions test whether you can reliably control model behavior in production — not
just write a clever one-off prompt.
Q. What is few-shot prompting, and when does it help vs.
hurt?
Few-shot prompting includes a small number of example (input, output) pairs in the prompt so the
model can infer the desired format, tone, or task pattern purely from context, without any weight
updates — this is called in-context learning.
It helps most for structured, non-obvious output formats (specific JSON schemas, unusual
classification labels, style matching) where instructions alone are ambiguous.
It can hurt when examples are too similar to each other and cause the model to overfit to surface
patterns instead of the underlying task, when examples are low-quality (the model will faithfully
imitate mistakes), or when it simply eats context budget better spent on retrieved knowledge for
a RAG-heavy task. Order and diversity of examples also measurably affects output — this is a
well-documented instability in in-context learning.
FOUNDATIONAL
Q. Explain Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and why it
improves performance on reasoning tasks.
CoT prompting asks the model to produce intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer
(e.g., 'Let's think step by step'), rather than jumping directly to a conclusion.
It helps because it gives the model more forward computation and 'working memory' in the form
of tokens it can condition on — the model effectively gets to reason token-by-token instead of
having to compress a multi-step derivation into a single forward pass. It's most impactful on
arithmetic, logic, and multi-step reasoning tasks, and shows little to no benefit on simple factual
recall.
Zero-shot CoT ('think step by step') vs few-shot CoT (showing worked examples with reasoning)
are both common; few-shot CoT generally performs better but costs more context tokens.
FOUNDATIONAL
Q. What is self-consistency, and how does it improve on
plain Chain-of-Thought?
Self-consistency samples multiple independent reasoning paths for the same question (using
temperature > 0 so each generation differs), then takes a majority vote over the final answers
instead of trusting a single greedy chain of reasoning.
The intuition: a single CoT trace can go down a wrong reasoning path and still sound confident,
but wrong paths tend to disagree with each other while correct reasoning tends to converge on
the same answer from different angles. This measurably improves accuracy on arithmetic and
logical reasoning benchmarks at the cost of running inference N times instead of once — a
latency/cost tradeoff worth naming explicitly in an interview answer.
INTERMEDIATE

Answer: Q. How do you reliably get structured (e.g., JSON) output
from an LLM in production?
The most reliable approach is constrained decoding / structured output modes (e.g., function
calling or a JSON-schema-constrained generation mode) where the model's token sampling is
actually restricted at each step to only tokens that keep the output valid against the schema —
this guarantees syntactic validity, unlike asking nicely in a prompt.
When constrained decoding isn't available, the fallback pattern is: provide the schema and a
concrete example in the prompt, ask for JSON only with no surrounding prose, parse the output
defensively, and automatically retry with the parse error fed back to the model if it fails validation
— capped at a small number of retries with a fallback path (e.g., escalate or return a default) if it
keeps failing.
Common mistake to flag in an interview: relying purely on prompt instructions ('respond only in
JSON') without any validation/retry layer — this works most of the time in a demo and then breaks
unpredictably in production traffic.
INTERMEDIATE
Q. When would you use prompt chaining (multiple LLM calls)
instead of one large complex prompt?
Prompt chaining breaks a complex task into a sequence of smaller, focused LLM calls, where each
step's output feeds the next — e.g., extract → classify → summarize → format, rather than asking
one prompt to do all four at once.
It helps when a single prompt asking for too much at once degrades quality (the model has to
juggle many instructions simultaneously and something gets dropped), when different steps
benefit from different models (a cheap model for extraction, an expensive one for the hard
reasoning step), or when you need visibility/control at intermediate steps for debugging,
validation, or human review.
The tradeoff is added latency (multiple sequential round-trips) and cost, plus more places for
errors to compound across the chain — so it's a deliberate architecture decision, not a default. A
good answer frames it as: chain when task decomposition genuinely improves reliability or
control; keep it a single call when the task is simple enough that decomposition only adds latency
without a quality benefit.
INTERMEDIATE

Answer: Q. What is the difference between prompt engineering, RAG,
and fine-tuning — how do you decide which to use?
Prompt engineering shapes behavior at inference time with no model or knowledge changes —
cheapest and fastest to iterate, best for format/style/reasoning-strategy control, but limited by
context window and can't inject knowledge the model wasn't trained on reliably.
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) injects external, up-to-date, or proprietary knowledge into
the prompt at query time via retrieval — solves the knowledge-freshness and hallucination-on-
facts problem without retraining, and keeps a clear citation trail back to source documents.
Fine-tuning changes the model's weights — best when you need to change behavior/style/format
consistently at scale (so you don't have to re-explain it every prompt), teach a new skill or domain
vocabulary, or reduce latency/cost by baking instructions into weights instead of a long system
prompt. It does NOT reliably fix hallucination or add real-time knowledge.
The standard interview answer: start with prompt engineering, add RAG when you need

Answer: Q. How would you handle a very long input that exceeds the
model's context window?
Map-reduce summarization: split the input into chunks, summarize each independently, then
summarize the summaries (recursively, if needed) — works well for tasks like 'summarize this
300-page document.'
Refine/iterative: process chunks sequentially, updating a running answer/summary with each new
chunk's information — preserves more nuance than map-reduce but is inherently sequential and
slower.

only the most relevant portions of the input for the specific question being asked, rather than
processing the whole document for every query.

right tool — but even then, be ready to discuss the 'lost in the middle' effect, where models attend
less reliably to information buried in the middle of a very long context versus the beginning or
end.

Q. How do you design a robust system prompt for a
production application?
Be explicit and structured: define the role/persona, the task boundaries (what it should and
shouldn't do), the output format (with an example), and how to handle edge cases (missing info,

plain Chain-of-Thought?
ReAct (Reason + Act) interleaves reasoning traces with concrete actions (tool calls) and
observations: the model reasons about what to do, takes an action (e.g., calls a search API),
observes the result, and reasons again — repeating until it reaches a final answer.
Plain CoT reasons entirely from the model's internal knowledge with no way to fetch new
information or verify facts mid-reasoning. ReAct grounds reasoning in real-world feedback at each
step, which is why it's the foundational pattern behind most agentic tool-use frameworks — the
reasoning trace itself gets corrected by what the tools actually return, reducing compounding

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
RAG is the single most commonly built GenAI system in industry. Expect deep, practical questions here
— interviewers want to know you've actually debugged a retrieval pipeline, not just read about one.
Q. Describe the end-to-end RAG pipeline.
Ingestion (offline): documents are loaded, cleaned, and split into chunks; each chunk is passed
through an embedding model to produce a dense vector; vectors + metadata are stored in a
vector database (or hybrid store) with an index for fast similarity search.
Retrieval (online, per query): the user query is embedded with the same embedding model, the
vector store is searched for the top-k most similar chunks (often combined with keyword/BM25
search — hybrid retrieval), and results are optionally re-ranked with a cross-encoder for higher
precision.
Generation: retrieved chunks are inserted into the prompt as context, alongside the user's
question and system instructions, and the LLM generates a grounded answer — ideally with
citations back to the source chunks.

Q. What chunking strategy would you use, and what are the
tradeoffs of chunk size?
Fixed-size chunking (e.g., 512 tokens with 10-20% overlap) is simple and predictable but can split
sentences or ideas mid-thought. Recursive/semantic chunking respects natural boundaries —
paragraphs, sections, headers — and generally produces more coherent, self-contained chunks.
Document-structure-aware chunking (splitting on markdown headers, table boundaries) is
essential for structured docs.
Small chunks improve retrieval precision (each chunk is topically focused, so similarity search is
sharper) but risk losing surrounding context needed to answer the question, and can fragment a
single idea across multiple chunks. Large chunks preserve context and coherence but dilute the
embedding's specificity (a long chunk about many things embeds to a 'blurry' average vector) and
burn more of the context window per retrieved item.
A strong practical answer mentions parent-document / small-to-big retrieval: embed small chunks
for precise matching, but return the larger parent section or surrounding context to the LLM for
generation — getting retrieval precision and generation context simultaneously.

pattern' — followed by a concrete example. That signals real experience over textbook knowledge.

Answer: Q. How do you handle conflicting information across
retrieved sources in a RAG system?
First, surface the conflict rather than silently picking one side — instruct the model explicitly to
note when retrieved sources disagree and, where possible, attribute each claim to its specific
source rather than presenting a single blended answer as fact.
Use source metadata to help resolve conflicts programmatically where possible: recency (prefer
newer documents for time-sensitive facts), source authority/trust tier (an official policy doc should
usually outrank a Slack message in the same index), and document versioning so superseded
content can be filtered out or down-weighted at retrieval time rather than left to the LLM to
adjudicate.
This is also a strong argument for maintaining data hygiene in the underlying corpus —
deduplication and deprecation of stale documents at ingestion time prevents many conflicts from
ever reaching the retrieval stage at all, which is more reliable than trying to resolve them post-hoc
in the prompt.

Freshness and maintainability: updating a vector index when a document changes is far simpler
and cheaper than re-processing a giant static context, and avoids needing to re-run everything
through the model just to reflect one changed fact.
Precision and traceability: retrieval gives an explicit, auditable set of source chunks a claim is
grounded in; even with a large context window, models are demonstrably less reliable at
pinpointing and using information buried in the middle of a huge context ('lost in the middle') than
at using information surfaced by targeted retrieval.

into context makes it much harder to enforce document-level access control cleanly. In practice,
many production systems use both — RAG to narrow down to a relevant working set, with a longer
context window as headroom rather than a replacement for retrieval.

Fine-Tuning & PEFT
Fine-tuning questions probe whether you understand the cost/benefit tradeoffs and the mechanics well
enough to actually run a training job, not just cite technique names.
Q. What is LoRA, and why is it so widely used for fine-tuning
LLMs?
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes all original model weights and injects small trainable low-rank
matrices (A and B, where the update is approximated as ΔW = BA, with rank r much smaller than
the original dimensions) alongside key weight matrices, typically the attention projection layers.
This works because weight updates during fine-tuning tend to have a low 'intrinsic rank' — the
meaningful change needed to adapt a model to a new task doesn't require updating every
parameter with full freedom. By training only the small A/B matrices, LoRA cuts trainable
parameters by orders of magnitude (often <1% of the full model).
Practical benefits: far less GPU memory needed (no optimizer states for frozen weights), much
faster training, small checkpoint sizes (megabytes instead of gigabytes) making it easy to
store/swap many task-specific adapters, and at inference time the adapter can be merged back
into the base weights with zero added latency.
FOUNDATIONAL
Q. What is QLoRA, and how does it differ from standard
LoRA?
QLoRA combines LoRA with 4-bit quantization of the frozen base model weights (using a
specialized 4-bit NormalFloat data type designed for normally-distributed weights), plus double
quantization and paged optimizers to manage memory spikes.
The base model stays frozen and quantized to 4-bit (drastically cutting memory footprint), while
the small LoRA adapter matrices are still trained in higher precision (typically BF16), and gradients
flow through the quantized weights during backprop without ever fully dequantizing them into
memory.
This is what made it practical to fine-tune large models (65B+ parameters) on a single
consumer/prosumer GPU, and is now a default choice whenever GPU memory is the binding
constraint for a fine-tuning job.

Answer: Q. When should you fine-tune vs. rely on prompting/RAG?
Give a concrete example.
Fine-tune when: you need a consistent output format/style at scale without repeating lengthy
instructions every call (reducing prompt-token cost and latency), you're teaching a narrow skill the
base model does poorly even with good prompting (e.g., a very specific structured extraction
schema, or a domain-specific classification task with many labels), or you need to bake in a
tone/persona very reliably.
Don't fine-tune to add knowledge — this is a very common mistake. Fine-tuning teaches patterns
and behavior, but is a poor and expensive way to inject new facts reliably; models fine-tuned on
new facts can still hallucinate or misremember them, whereas RAG retrieves facts at query time
with a verifiable source. Fine-tuning also doesn't handle facts that change after training without
retraining.
Concrete example: a customer support bot that must always output a structured JSON ticket-
classification with 40 highly specific internal categories is a good fine-tuning candidate (a narrow,
repeated, format-heavy skill). A bot answering questions about your company's constantly-
updated product documentation is a RAG candidate, not a fine-tuning one.
INTERMEDIATE
Q. What is catastrophic forgetting, and how do you mitigate
it during fine-tuning?
Catastrophic forgetting is when fine-tuning on a narrow new task degrades the model's previously
strong general capabilities — e.g., a model fine-tuned heavily on customer-support tickets
becomes worse at general reasoning or coding than the base model was.
Mitigations: use PEFT methods like LoRA instead of full fine-tuning, since freezing most weights
naturally limits how much general behavior can shift; mix a portion of general-purpose/instruction
data into the fine-tuning set alongside the task-specific data, so the model doesn't over-specialize;
use a lower learning rate and fewer epochs (over-training on a small dataset is the most common
cause); and evaluate on held-out general benchmarks — not just the target task — before and
after fine-tuning to catch regressions early.

production use?
Quality over quantity: a few thousand high-quality, diverse, correctly-labeled examples reliably
outperform a much larger noisy dataset — LLMs are sensitive to label noise during fine-tuning,
since it directly teaches the pattern you're optimizing for.
Ensure diversity across edge cases, input lengths, and phrasing so the model generalizes rather
than memorizing surface patterns; deduplicate near-identical examples, which otherwise bias
training and can cause overfitting/memorization.
Hold out a representative validation and test split before training (not just train/loss curves) and
build a small human-reviewed evaluation set that mirrors real production traffic patterns, since
offline loss metrics often don't correlate well with real-world output quality.

Almost every GenAI system relies on embeddings somewhere. These questions test whether you
understand what a vector actually represents and how retrieval infrastructure scales.
Q. What is an embedding, and what determines embedding
quality for a given task?
An embedding is a dense numerical vector representation of text (or image/audio) in a high-
dimensional space, produced by a model trained so that semantically similar inputs map to nearby
vectors (typically measured by cosine similarity or dot product).
Quality depends on: what the embedding model was trained on (domain match matters — a
general web-trained embedding model may perform poorly on legal or medical jargon vs. a
domain-tuned one), the training objective (contrastive learning on similar/dissimilar pairs is
standard), dimensionality (higher isn't always better — it raises storage/compute cost and can add
noise), and whether it's evaluated with a task-relevant benchmark like MTEB rather than assumed
from vendor marketing alone.
FOUNDATIONAL
Q. Compare HNSW, IVF, and exact (brute-force) search for
vector similarity search.
Brute-force / exact search compares the query vector to every vector in the dataset — perfectly
accurate (100% recall) but O(n) per query, which becomes too slow at scale (millions+ of vectors).
IVF (Inverted File Index) clusters vectors into partitions (via k-means) at index time; at query time,
it only searches the nearest few clusters instead of the whole dataset — much faster, with a
tunable accuracy/speed tradeoff via the number of clusters probed, but requires a
training/clustering step and can miss results near cluster boundaries.
HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a multi-layer graph structure where each vector
is a node connected to its approximate nearest neighbors; search greedily traverses from sparse
upper layers down to dense lower layers, achieving excellent recall/speed tradeoffs and is the
most widely used ANN algorithm in modern vector databases (default in most of them). Its main
cost is memory (graph structure overhead) and slower index build/insert time compared to IVF.
All three trade off recall vs. latency vs. memory vs. build time — approximate methods (HNSW,
IVF) are what make sub-100ms search over billions of vectors feasible in production, at the cost of
a small, tunable amount of retrieval accuracy versus exact search.

AI Agents & Orchestration
Agent questions are increasingly central to GenAI engineering interviews as products move from single-
turn Q&A to multi-step autonomous workflows.
Q. What defines an 'agent' as opposed to a simple LLM call
or a fixed pipeline?
An agent uses an LLM to dynamically decide its own sequence of actions — which tools to call, in
what order, and when to stop — based on intermediate results, rather than following a hardcoded,
predetermined sequence of steps.
The defining loop is typically: observe (current state/context) → reason (what should I do next?) →
act (call a tool, retrieve information, or respond) → observe the result → repeat until a stopping
condition is met. This is what enables agents to handle open-ended tasks a fixed pipeline can't
anticipate in advance.
A useful interview framing: a RAG pipeline is a fixed workflow (retrieve, then generate); an agentic
RAG system decides for itself whether to retrieve, what to search for, whether the results are
sufficient, and whether to search again — the control flow itself is delegated to the model.
FOUNDATIONAL
Q. How does function/tool calling actually work under the
hood?
The application provides the model with a set of tool definitions (name, description, and a JSON-
schema of expected parameters) alongside the prompt. The model is trained/fine-tuned to
recognize when a user request maps to one of these tools and to output a structured call — the
tool name plus arguments matching the schema — instead of (or alongside) natural language.
Critically, the model does not execute the tool itself — it only generates the structured intent to
call it. The application code parses that structured output, actually executes the function/API call,
and then feeds the result back into the conversation as a new message so the model can
incorporate it into its next response or decide on a next action.
This separation is a key safety property: the model proposes, but the application (and its
permission/validation layer) disposes — giving engineers a checkpoint to validate arguments,
enforce authorization, or require human approval before anything actually executes.

Answer: Q. What's the difference between short-term and long-term

each?
Short-term (working) memory is the current conversation/task context — typically just the recent
message history and intermediate reasoning/tool results within the active session, held directly in

or facts learned in earlier interactions — and is usually implemented outside the context window
entirely: stored in a database or vector store, and selectively retrieved (via similarity search or
explicit lookup) into the prompt only when relevant to the current turn, rather than kept
permanently in context.

older turns are compressed into a running summary to control context length, while specific

LLMOps, Deployment & Cost
This is where 'can you actually run this in production' gets tested — latency, cost, reliability, and
observability.
Q. What levers do you have to reduce LLM inference cost
and latency in production?
Model selection: use the smallest/cheapest model that meets your quality bar for each task rather
than one large model for everything — model routing (a lightweight classifier or the LLM itself
deciding task difficulty and picking a cheaper model for simple requests) is a widely used cost
lever.
Caching: cache exact or semantically-similar repeated queries/responses; prompt caching (reusing
the KV cache for a static system prompt or shared context prefix across requests) cuts both cost
and time-to-first-token significantly for high-repetition workloads.
Serving optimizations: batching concurrent requests, quantization, speculative decoding (a small
draft model proposes several tokens which the large model verifies in parallel, reducing sequential
forward passes), and using optimized inference servers (vLLM, TGI) with techniques like
PagedAttention for efficient KV-cache memory management.
Prompt/context efficiency: trim unnecessary context, use concise system prompts (or fine-tune to
bake in long instructions), and cap max output tokens where a shorter response is acceptable —
since both input and output tokens are billed and impact latency.
INTERMEDIATE
Q. How do you monitor an LLM application in production?
What should trigger an alert?
Track: latency (p50/p95/p99, and time-to-first-token for streaming UX), error/failure rates (API
errors, timeouts, malformed structured outputs), cost per request and daily spend trends, and
token usage patterns (input/output ratio, unusually long contexts).
Quality signals: automated groundedness/faithfulness scoring on a sample of live traffic, user
feedback signals (thumbs up/down, regeneration rate, session abandonment), and drift detection
— is the distribution of inputs or model behavior changing over time relative to your evaluation
baseline?
Alerting should be tied to concrete thresholds tied to user/business impact: latency SLA breaches,
error rate spikes, cost anomalies (e.g., a prompt-injection loop causing runaway token usage), and
sudden drops in user satisfaction signals — not just raw uptime, since an LLM system can be 'up'
while silently producing degraded or unsafe outputs.

Answer: Q. What is LLM observability/tracing, and why is it different
from traditional software observability?
Traditional observability (logs, metrics, traces) tracks deterministic code paths — the same input
reliably produces the same trace. LLM systems are non-deterministic and often involve multi-step
chains (retrieval → re-ranking → generation → tool calls → possibly more generation), so a trace
needs to capture the full reasoning path: every prompt sent, every intermediate output, every tool
call and its result, token counts, and latency at each hop.
This granularity is what makes debugging possible — when an agent produces a wrong answer,
you need to see exactly which retrieval returned poor results, which prompt version was used, and
what the model actually reasoned through, not just an input/output pair. Tools like LangSmith,
Langfuse, and Arize Phoenix exist specifically to capture and visualize these multi-step traces,
which off-the-shelf APM tools weren't built for.
INTERMEDIATE
Q. How do you safely roll out a change to a prompt or model
version in a production LLM application?
Version and evaluate offline first: run the change against a held-out evaluation set (including
known edge cases and past regression examples) and compare quality/cost/latency metrics
against the current production version before considering deployment.
Roll out gradually: canary or A/B test the change on a small percentage of live traffic, monitor the
same quality/cost/safety signals as full production monitoring, and have an instant rollback path
(treat prompts and model versions as deployable artifacts with the same rigor as code).
Keep prompts under version control alongside application code, and maintain a regression suite
that runs automatically on every prompt/model change — this catches the common failure mode
where a prompt tweak fixes one case but silently breaks several others.

Q. How would you design fallback/failover when your
primary LLM provider has an outage or is rate-limiting
you?
Maintain a fallback chain to a secondary provider/model for critical paths, with request routing
logic that detects failures (timeouts, 5xx errors, rate-limit responses) and automatically retries
against the fallback rather than surfacing an error straight to the user.
This requires keeping prompts reasonably portable across providers (or maintaining provider-
specific prompt variants) since models don't behave identically to the same prompt, and testing
the fallback path regularly — a failover mechanism that's never been exercised often turns out to
be broken exactly when you need it.
For rate limits specifically: implement client-side request queuing/backoff and exponential retry
with jitter, and consider tiered degradation (e.g., serve a smaller/faster model or a cached
response under load rather than fully failing) so the user experience degrades gracefully instead
of breaking outright.

Streaming sends generated tokens to the client incrementally as they're produced (typically via

complete before returning anything — the client renders tokens as they arrive.

to-first-token can be a few hundred milliseconds even if total generation takes several seconds, so
streaming makes the application feel dramatically more responsive even though the total time to
full completion is unchanged.

stream (you generally can't parse or validate JSON until it's complete, so structured-output and

Evaluation, Safety & Guardrails
Increasingly a dedicated interview section on its own — companies want to know you take output quality
and safety seriously, not just capability.
Q. What is LLM-as-judge, and what are its known failure
modes?
LLM-as-judge uses a (typically stronger) LLM to evaluate the outputs of another LLM against a
rubric — e.g., scoring helpfulness, correctness, or faithfulness — which scales far better than
manual human review and is now standard for offline eval pipelines and even some online quality
monitoring.
Known failure modes: position bias (favoring whichever response appears first when comparing
two outputs — mitigated by randomizing/swapping order), self-preference bias (a judge model
tends to rate outputs from its own model family more favorably), verbosity bias (longer answers
often score higher regardless of actual quality), and sensitivity to how the rubric/prompt is
worded.
Best practice: validate the judge itself against a smaller human-labeled gold set periodically to
confirm it correlates well with human judgment, use clear rubrics with concrete scoring criteria
rather than vague quality questions, and don't treat LLM-judge scores as ground truth in isolation
— combine with human spot-checks, especially for high-stakes decisions.
INTERMEDIATE
Q. What are guardrails, and what are the main categories
you'd implement in a production GenAI system?
Guardrails are checks placed around an LLM's inputs and/or outputs to enforce safety,
correctness, and policy constraints beyond what prompting alone reliably guarantees.
Input guardrails: PII detection/redaction, prompt injection/jailbreak detection, topic/scope filtering
(rejecting clearly out-of-scope requests before they reach the model), and rate limiting/abuse
detection.
Output guardrails: toxicity/harmful content filtering, structured output validation (does the
response match the required schema — regenerate or fall back if not), factuality/groundedness
checks for RAG-grounded answers, and PII leakage checks before returning a response to the
user.
Architecturally, these are usually implemented as separate lightweight classifiers or rule-based
checks that run before/after the main LLM call — not baked into the main model's prompt alone —
because a single prompt asking the model to 'also be careful about X' is much less reliable than a
dedicated, independently-tested check.

Classical ML & Deep Learning
Fundamentals
Even GenAI-focused loops often open with core ML/DL fundamentals to confirm the basics are solid
before going deep on transformers. Don't skip this section assuming it's 'too basic' — a shaky answer
here is a fast, avoidable way to lose credibility early in the interview.
Q. Explain the bias-variance tradeoff. How do you diagnose
whether a model is overfitting or underfitting?
Bias is error from overly simplistic assumptions (the model can't capture the true pattern even
with unlimited data); variance is error from being overly sensitive to the specific training set (the
model captures noise, not just signal). Total generalization error decomposes roughly into bias² +
variance + irreducible noise, and the two typically trade off against each other as model
complexity changes.
Underfitting (high bias) shows up as poor performance on both training and validation/test data —
the model is too simple to fit even the training set well. Overfitting (high variance) shows up as
strong training performance but a large, widening gap to validation/test performance — the model
has memorized training-specific noise instead of learning generalizable patterns.
Diagnosis in practice: plot training vs. validation loss curves over training steps/epochs — a
widening gap is the classic overfitting signature. Fixes for overfitting include more data,
regularization (dropout, weight decay, early stopping), or a simpler model; fixes for underfitting
include a more expressive model, more training time, or better features.
FOUNDATIONAL
Q. What is backpropagation, and how do optimizers like
SGD, Momentum, and Adam differ?
Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter in the
network by applying the chain rule backward through the computational graph, layer by layer —
this is what makes training deep networks with millions/billions of parameters tractable, since it
computes all gradients in a single backward pass rather than one at a time.
Plain SGD updates each parameter directly opposite its gradient, scaled by a learning rate —
simple, but can be slow and oscillate in narrow/curved loss landscapes. Momentum adds a running
average of past gradients to the update, which accelerates progress in consistent directions and
dampens oscillation, much like a ball rolling downhill picking up speed.
Adam combines momentum with an adaptive, per-parameter learning rate derived from a running
average of squared gradients — parameters with consistently large gradients get smaller effective
steps and vice versa. This adaptivity is why Adam (and variants like AdamW) is the default
optimizer for training most modern deep learning models, including LLMs, despite plain SGD
sometimes generalizing slightly better with careful tuning.
FOUNDATIONAL

exponentially as it propagates backward through many layers (vanishing), making early layers
barely update. If the factors are consistently greater than 1, the gradient grows exponentially
(exploding), causing unstable, huge parameter updates. Mitigations: residual/skip connections (used throughout Transformers) give gradients a direct,

activation magnitudes stable layer to layer; and gradient clipping caps the gradient norm to

Answer: Q. Precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC — when does each
metric matter most?
Precision = (true positives) / (predicted positives) — of everything the model flagged as positive,
how much was actually correct. Matters most when false positives are costly (e.g., a fraud-
flagging system that blocks legitimate transactions too often erodes user trust).
Recall = (true positives) / (actual positives) — of everything that was actually positive, how much
did the model catch. Matters most when false negatives are costly (e.g., a content-moderation
classifier that misses genuinely harmful content is a worse failure than an occasional over-flag).
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, useful as a single balanced number when both
error types matter and especially when classes are imbalanced, since plain accuracy can look
deceptively high on an imbalanced dataset by just predicting the majority class.
ROC-AUC measures ranking quality across all possible classification thresholds — how well the
model separates positive from negative examples regardless of where you set the cutoff. It's
useful for comparing models independent of a specific operating threshold, but can be
misleadingly optimistic on heavily imbalanced datasets, where precision-recall AUC is usually the
more informative choice.
INTERMEDIATE

Multimodal Models & Diffusion
As GenAI products increasingly span text, image, audio, and video, expect at least a couple of questions
probing whether you understand what's structurally different about non-text modalities — even in a
primarily text/LLM-focused role.
Q. How do vision-language models like CLIP and LLaVA
actually work?
CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder jointly using contrastive learning: given a batch
of (image, caption) pairs, it pulls the embeddings of matching pairs closer together and pushes
non-matching pairs apart, so that at the end both modalities share a common embedding space
where semantically similar images and text land near each other — with no generative objective
at all, just alignment.
LLaVA-style models instead connect a pretrained vision encoder to a pretrained LLM: an image is
split into patches, embedded by a vision transformer (ViT) encoder, projected through a small
trainable adapter/projection layer into the same embedding dimension as the LLM's token
embeddings, and then fed into the LLM alongside text tokens — the model is then fine-tuned so it
learns to jointly attend to image-patch embeddings and text tokens as one unified sequence.
The key distinction to articulate in an interview: CLIP is fundamentally about alignment/retrieval
(are this image and this text related?), while LLaVA-style architectures are about generation
(produce text conditioned on both image and text input) — different objectives, and often used
together in a pipeline (CLIP-style encoders are frequently the vision backbone feeding into a
LLaVA-style generative model).
INTERMEDIATE
Q. Walk through how diffusion models generate images —
the forward and reverse process.
The forward process is fixed and not learned: starting from a real image, Gaussian noise is added
incrementally over many steps until the image becomes pure noise. This defines a known,
tractable path from data to noise.
The reverse process is what the model learns: a neural network (typically a U-Net, or a
Transformer-based DiT in newer models) is trained to predict and remove a small amount of noise
at each step, gradually denoising a random noise sample back into a coherent image over many
iterations.
Generation at inference time starts from pure random noise and repeatedly applies the learned
denoising step, guided by a conditioning signal (e.g., a text prompt embedding, typically via cross-
attention layers injected into the denoising network) — sampling a genuinely new image rather
than reconstructing a specific training example.
INTERMEDIATE

Answer: Q. What's the difference between diffusion models and GANs
for image generation?
GANs (Generative Adversarial Networks) train two networks adversarially: a generator that tries to
produce realistic images from random noise in a single forward pass, and a discriminator that tries
to distinguish generated images from real ones — the generator improves by learning to fool an
increasingly capable discriminator.
Diffusion models instead learn to iteratively denoise, requiring many sequential forward passes to
generate one image (though modern techniques have cut this down significantly), rather than
GANs' single-pass generation.
In practice: GANs are much faster at inference (one pass) but are notoriously unstable to train
(mode collapse, adversarial training dynamics that don't converge cleanly) and tend to produce
less diverse outputs. Diffusion models are slower per generation but train more stably, scale
better with data/compute, and currently produce higher-fidelity, more diverse results — which is
why diffusion architectures (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, Midjourney's underlying approach) have
become the dominant paradigm for state-of-the-art image generation, with GANs now more
common in specialized, latency-sensitive use cases.
ADVANCED
Q. How does a text-to-image pipeline like Stable Diffusion
actually work end-to-end?
A text encoder (typically a CLIP text encoder) converts the input prompt into an embedding that
captures its semantic content — this embedding will condition every step of the generation
process.
Rather than diffusing in raw pixel space (computationally very expensive for high-resolution
images), latent diffusion models first compress the image into a smaller latent representation
using a pretrained autoencoder (a VAE), and run the entire diffusion/denoising process in this
much lower-dimensional latent space — this is the key efficiency insight that made high-resolution
diffusion models practical to train and run.
A U-Net (or newer DiT/Transformer-based denoiser) then iteratively denoises a random latent, at
each step cross-attending to the text embedding so the denoising direction is guided by the
prompt, gradually shaping random noise into a latent that represents a coherent image.
Finally, the VAE decoder converts the denoised latent back into a full-resolution pixel-space
image. Being able to name this three-part structure — text encoder, latent-space diffusion U-Net,
VAE decoder — is usually what separates a candidate who has actually read the architecture from
one who's only used the product.
ADVANCED

Answer: Q. How are images actually tokenized or represented as
input to a multimodal LLM?
Unlike text, which has a natural discrete vocabulary, images are continuous pixel grids — so the
standard approach (following Vision Transformer/ViT) is to split the image into fixed-size patches
(e.g., 16×16 pixels), flatten each patch, and linearly project it into an embedding vector —
conceptually the image equivalent of a 'token,' though it represents a patch of pixels rather than a
discrete symbol.
These patch embeddings, plus positional information indicating where each patch sits in the
image, are then projected (often through a small trainable adapter) into the same embedding
space as the LLM's text token embeddings, so the model's self-attention can operate over a single
unified sequence mixing image-patch tokens and text tokens.
Some newer approaches use a learned tokenizer that maps image regions to a discrete codebook
(closer to true 'image tokens' analogous to text tokens, e.g., VQ-VAE-style approaches), which is
worth mentioning if the conversation goes deeper — but the patch-embedding-via-ViT approach is
the more common default in today's production multimodal LLMs.
INTERMEDIATE
Q. How do you evaluate the quality of generated images?
FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) compares the statistical distribution of features (extracted by a
pretrained classifier network) between a set of generated images and a set of real images — lower
FID means the generated distribution is closer to real image statistics, and it's the most widely
used automated metric for overall generation quality/realism.
CLIP score measures how well a generated image matches its text prompt, by embedding both
with CLIP and computing their similarity — this specifically evaluates prompt-
adherence/alignment, which FID does not capture at all (an image can look photorealistic yet
completely ignore the prompt).
Neither metric fully captures human aesthetic judgment or subtle failure modes (extra fingers,
broken text, physically implausible objects), so rigorous evaluation still pairs these automated
metrics with structured human evaluation — pairwise comparisons or rubric-based scoring by
human raters — especially before shipping a user-facing generation feature.

Infrastructure & Deployment Engineering
The LLMOps section covered the what and why of production cost, latency, and monitoring; this section
covers the how — the actual infrastructure decisions behind serving models reliably at scale.
Q. How would you containerize and deploy an LLM inference
service? What goes into the Docker image?
A production inference image typically includes: the serving framework (e.g., vLLM, TGI, or a
custom FastAPI wrapper around the model), pinned dependency versions (critical for
reproducibility — GPU/CUDA driver mismatches are one of the most common 'works on my
machine' failures in ML infra), and the model weights themselves — though for large models,
weights are often mounted from external storage or pulled at startup rather than baked into the
image, to keep image size and build times manageable.
The base image should match the CUDA/driver version the serving framework was built and tested
against, since GPU inference is far more sensitive to environment mismatches than typical
stateless web services. Health-check and readiness-probe endpoints matter more than usual here
too, since a model that's still loading weights into GPU memory needs to report 'not ready' rather
than accept and fail requests during startup.
INTERMEDIATE
Q. How do you use Kubernetes to scale a GPU-backed
inference service, and what's different from scaling
stateless web services?
GPUs are a scarce, expensive, and non-fungible resource compared to CPU/memory — Kubernetes
needs GPU device plugins to schedule pods onto nodes with available GPUs, and autoscaling has
to account for the fact that spinning up a new GPU node (and loading a large model's weights onto
it) can take minutes, not seconds, unlike a typical stateless web pod.
Standard CPU-utilization-based autoscaling often doesn't reflect real load for LLM serving —
request queue depth, GPU memory utilization, or custom metrics like tokens-per-second
throughput are usually better autoscaling signals than CPU percentage.
Because cold-start latency is so much higher for GPU workloads, teams often keep a warm
minimum replica count rather than scaling to zero, and use request queuing/batching at the
serving layer to absorb bursts without needing to scale hardware instantly. Model sharding across
multiple GPUs (for models too large for one GPU) adds further complexity — Kubernetes needs to
schedule sharded replicas as a coordinated group, not independent pods.
ADVANCED

Answer: Q. Serverless GPU inference vs. always-on dedicated servers
— how do you decide? Serverless GPU (pay-per-request, scales to zero) fits bursty, unpredictable, or low-volume traffic
well — you avoid paying for idle GPU time, at the cost of cold-start latency when a new instance
has to spin up and load model weights, which can be seconds to tens of seconds for large models. Always-on dedicated servers fit steady, predictable, high-volume traffic — you pay for capacity
whether or not it's fully utilized, but you eliminate cold-start latency entirely and get more
predictable performance, which matters a lot for latency-sensitive user-facing features. A common middle ground: a small warm pool of always-on capacity to absorb baseline traffic with
zero cold-start, with serverless or autoscaled capacity layered on top to absorb spikes — the
decision should be driven by your actual traffic shape (steady vs. bursty) and how latency-
sensitive the specific feature is, not a blanket policy across every service. INTERMEDIATE
Q. What is continuous batching, and why does it matter for
LLM serving throughput? Naive (static) batching groups a fixed set of requests together and waits for every request in the
batch to finish generating before processing the next batch — but LLM requests finish at very
different times (short answers finish fast, long answers take much longer), so static batching
wastes significant GPU capacity idling on requests that finished early while waiting for the slowest
one.

Answer: Continuous (dynamic) batching instead adds new incoming requests into the running batch as
soon as a slot frees up (i.e., as soon as any request in the batch finishes), keeping the GPU
consistently saturated with useful work rather than idling — this is one of the single biggest
throughput improvements in modern LLM serving frameworks (vLLM, TGI) compared to naive
batching, often multiplying achievable throughput several times over on the same hardware. ADVANCED
Q. What's the difference between tensor parallelism and
pipeline parallelism for serving very large models across
multiple GPUs? Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices/layers across multiple GPUs — e.g., a single
attention or feed-forward layer's computation is divided across GPUs, which must communicate
(all-reduce) after every split operation. This requires very fast interconnects (like NVLink) between
GPUs since communication happens constantly within a single forward pass, but it keeps latency
low since all GPUs work on the same request simultaneously. Pipeline parallelism instead assigns different full layers to different GPUs (GPU 1 handles layers 1–
10, GPU 2 handles layers 11–20, etc.), passing activations between GPUs sequentially as data
flows through the layers — this needs far less inter-GPU communication bandwidth than tensor
parallelism, but can leave GPUs idle waiting for the previous stage (a 'pipeline bubble') unless
carefully scheduled with overlapping micro-batches. In practice, serving very large models often combines both: tensor parallelism within a node
(where GPUs have fast NVLink interconnects) and pipeline parallelism across nodes (where inter-
node bandwidth is more limited) — knowing when and why to combine them is a strong signal of
real infrastructure experience.

Answer: Q. How do you design load balancing and routing across
multiple model replicas or multiple providers?
Within a single model's replicas: route based on actual load signals (queue depth, current KV-
cache/memory utilization) rather than simple round-robin, since LLM requests have wildly varying
costs (a 50-token vs. 4000-token generation) that round-robin doesn't account for — least-loaded
routing generally outperforms round-robin for this reason.
Across multiple providers/models (e.g., a primary and fallback provider, or routing between a large
and small model by task difficulty): implement health-check-based failover so a struggling
provider is automatically routed around, and consider weighted routing to gradually shift traffic
during a migration or A/B test rather than an abrupt full cutover.
Sticky sessions can matter for multi-turn conversations if server-side state (like an uncommitted
KV cache for a long-running session) is tied to a specific replica — otherwise, requests should
generally be treated as stateless and freely routable to whichever replica has capacity.

Coding & Practical Exercises
Many GenAI engineer loops still include a live or take-home coding round. These exercises cover the
building blocks that come up repeatedly — retrieval, chunking, resilience patterns, and agent control
flow — with the reasoning an interviewer is actually listening for, not just a working solution.
CODING EXERCISE
Implement cosine similarity search over a list of embeddings.
This is the retrieval building block behind almost every RAG system. The key things an interviewer is checking:
do you normalize vectors correctly, do you avoid an O(n²) mistake, and can you reason about doing this at
scale (this naive version is O(n) per query — mention that production systems replace this linear scan with an
ANN index like HNSW once the corpus grows past a few thousand vectors).
import numpy as np
def cosine_similarity(query: np.ndarray, corpus: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
 """query: shape (d,) corpus: shape (n, d) returns: shape (n,)"""
 query_norm = query / (np.linalg.norm(query) + 1e-10)
 corpus_norm = corpus / (np.linalg.norm(corpus, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-10)
 return corpus_norm @ query_norm
def top_k(query: np.ndarray, corpus: np.ndarray, k: int = 5) -> list[int]:
 scores = cosine_similarity(query, corpus)
 return list(np.argsort(-scores)[:k])
CODING EXERCISE
Write a text-chunking function with configurable chunk size and overlap.
Interviewers are checking whether you handle the overlap logic correctly (a common off-by-one source of
bugs), whether you guard against an infinite loop when overlap ≥ chunk size, and whether you're thinking in
tokens vs. characters (this sketch chunks by characters for simplicity — mention you'd swap in a tokenizer's
encode/decode for production accuracy).
def chunk_text(text: str, chunk_size: int = 500, overlap: int = 50) -> list[str]:
 if overlap >= chunk_size:
 raise ValueError("overlap must be smaller than chunk_size")
 chunks = []
 start = 0
 while start < len(text):
 end = start + chunk_size
 chunks.append(text[start:end])
 start += chunk_size - overlap
 return chunks

Write a token-bucket rate limiter for outgoing API calls.
This is checking whether you understand token-bucket vs. fixed-window rate limiting (token bucket allows brief
bursts up to the bucket size while still enforcing a long-run average rate, which better matches how most LLM
provider rate limits actually behave) and whether your refill logic is time-based and correct rather than a hacky
counter reset.
import time
class TokenBucket:
 def __init__(self, rate: float, capacity: int):
 self.rate = rate # tokens added per second
 self.capacity = capacity
 self.tokens = capacity
 self.last_refill = time.monotonic()
 def _refill(self):
 now = time.monotonic()
 elapsed = now - self.last_refill
 self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + elapsed * self.rate)
 self.last_refill = now
 def allow(self) -> bool:
 self._refill()
 if self.tokens >= 1:
 self.tokens -= 1
 return True
 return False
CODING EXERCISE
Sketch the core loop of a ReAct-style agent with tool calling.
This is a systems-design-through-code question — interviewers want to see the reason → act → observe loop
structured cleanly, an explicit max-iteration cap (a very common thing candidates forget), and a clear
separation between 'the model decided to call a tool' and 'the application actually executes it,' which is the
safety-relevant boundary discussed in the Agents section.
def run_agent(user_input: str, tools: dict, max_steps: int = 8) -> str:
 messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_input}]
 for step in range(max_steps):
 response = llm_call(messages, tools=list(tools.keys()))
 if response.tool_call is None:
 return response.content # model produced a final answer
 tool_name = response.tool_call.name
 tool_args = response.tool_call.arguments
 if tool_name not in tools:
 messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": f"Unknown tool: {tool_name}"})
 continue
 result = tools[tool_name](**tool_args) # application executes, not the model
 messages.append({"role": "assistant", "tool_call": response.tool_call})
 messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": str(result)})
 return "Max steps reached without a final answer."

Scenario-Based Questions
These simulate the "here's a mess, walk me through your triage" questions that senior GenAI interviews
increasingly favor over textbook recall. Interviewers are scoring your diagnostic process — where you
look first, how you isolate root cause, and what structural fix you'd ship — as much as the final answer.
SCENARIO
Users report that the chatbot gives noticeably different answers to the exact
same question when asked minutes apart. How do you debug this?
First isolate the variable: check temperature/sampling settings (T > 0 will naturally produce different
phrasing and sometimes different substance run to run) versus an actual retrieval instability (is the
RAG pipeline returning different chunks for the same query, e.g., due to a recently updated index or
a non-deterministic re-ranker).
Check for a silent model or prompt version change — an unpinned model alias, an auto-updated
provider model, or an A/B test the requester wasn't told about are common culprits that look like
'random' inconsistency but are actually deterministic version drift.
If it's genuinely sampling variance and consistency matters for this use case, lower temperature
toward 0 for factual/deterministic tasks, or add a caching layer for repeated identical queries.
Add this exact case to your regression eval set once resolved, and consider logging model/prompt
version alongside every response so 'it gave a different answer' is always trivially explainable after
the fact.
SCENARIO
Production latency for your LLM feature suddenly tripled with no code deploy
and no traffic spike. Walk through your triage.
Check provider-side status first (is this an upstream outage/degradation, not your system) —
provider dashboards and status pages before assuming the problem is internal.
Look at token counts: has average input or output length grown (e.g., a retrieval change now
returns more/larger chunks, or conversation histories have grown longer than usual) — latency
scales with token count, so a silent increase in context size is a very common root cause.
Check for a model routing change (did a fallback path kick in to a slower model), a KV-
cache/batching regression on self-hosted infra, or a downstream dependency (vector DB, re-ranker
service) that got slow and is now the bottleneck in the chain rather than the LLM call itself.
Isolate with tracing: break down end-to-end latency by stage (retrieval, re-ranking, generation, post-
processing) rather than treating 'the LLM call' as one black box — this is exactly what LLM
observability tooling is for.

Answer: SCENARIO
Monthly LLM API spend has tripled over three months while user traffic has
stayed roughly flat. How do you investigate and fix it?
Break spend down by endpoint/feature and by token type (input vs. output) — a single feature or a
single growing conversation-history pattern is often responsible for the bulk of the increase, not a
broad uniform rise.
Check for context growth: are conversation histories, RAG context sizes, or few-shot examples
silently growing over time (e.g., an unbounded conversation history being replayed in full on every
turn)?
Check for retry/loop inflation: a bug causing duplicate calls, an agent looping more than expected,
or a fallback path being hit far more often than intended can multiply cost without a visible traffic
change.
Once diagnosed, apply targeted fixes: cap/truncate or summarize long histories, add prompt
caching for repeated static context, and consider model routing so only genuinely hard requests use
the most expensive model.
SCENARIO
Vector search returns irrelevant results specifically for short, acronym-heavy
technical queries, while longer natural-language queries work fine. Diagnose it.
This is a classic dense-retrieval weakness: embedding models often struggle with short queries and
rare acronyms/proper nouns because there's little semantic context for the model to embed
meaningfully, and the acronym may barely appear in the training data of the embedding model.
Check whether hybrid search (adding BM25/keyword matching) is enabled — sparse retrieval
typically handles exact acronym/term matching far better than dense embeddings alone, and this
symptom pattern is almost a textbook case for why hybrid search exists.
Consider query expansion for short queries (e.g., using the LLM itself to expand an acronym or
rephrase a terse query into a fuller semantic query before embedding it) as a complementary fix.
Validate with a targeted eval slice: build a small test set specifically of short/acronym queries and
measure retrieval metrics on that slice separately, since it can look fine in aggregate metrics while
being broken for this specific query type.

System Design Case Studies
Senior GenAI engineer interviews almost always include one open-ended design question. These three
walkthroughs model the structure and depth expected: ingestion/retrieval architecture, safety
guardrails, and evaluation strategy — not just a model name.
Design a customer-support chatbot grounded in a company's help-
center documentation
Ingestion: scrape/sync help-center articles, chunk by section headers, embed with a domain-
appropriate model, index in a hybrid (dense + BM25) vector store; set up a re-indexing pipeline to
catch article updates.
Retrieval: hybrid search + cross-encoder re-ranking, top-3–5 chunks passed to the LLM with citations
required in the output.
Guardrails: scope classifier to reject off-topic questions, PII redaction on user input, faithfulness
check before returning an answer, and a confident 'I don't know, let me connect you to a human'
fallback when retrieval confidence is low.
Escalation: clear handoff to a human agent with full conversation context when the bot is uncertain
or the user explicitly asks for a human.
Evaluation: golden set of real support tickets with correct answers, tracking faithfulness, resolution
rate, and escalation rate over time; online A/B testing before rolling out prompt/model changes.
Design a code-generation copilot for an internal engineering team
Context assembly: retrieve relevant code from the repo (via embeddings over code chunks +
symbol/dependency graph awareness), include open files, recent edits, and relevant style/lint config
in the prompt.
Model choice: a code-specialized model (or a general model fine-tuned/prompted with few-shot
examples of the team's code style); consider a smaller, faster model for inline autocomplete vs. a
larger model for chat-based multi-file tasks.
Safety: never auto-execute generated code without review; static analysis / lint / test-run as a
validation gate before suggesting a change is 'ready.'
Latency: autocomplete needs sub-200ms time-to-first-token — this pushes toward smaller models,
aggressive caching of repo context, and streaming generation.
Evaluation: acceptance rate of suggestions, downstream bug rate in accepted suggestions, and
developer time-saved surveys — not just code-generation benchmark scores in isolation.

Structured extraction: define a strict JSON schema for required fields, use function-calling/structured-
output mode rather than free-text parsing, and validate output against the schema with automatic
retry on failure.

verification pass — e.g., regex/rule-based cross-check, or a second LLM call specifically verifying
each extracted field is directly quoted/traceable to the source text.
Human-in-the-loop: route low-confidence extractions to human review rather than silently guessing,
given the cost of an error in a legal/financial context.
Cost: batch processing with a cheaper model where accuracy allows, reserving the most capable
(and expensive) model for the highest-stakes documents or fields.

Project & Portfolio Questions
These questions ask you to narrate your own work. The difference between a strong and weak answer is
almost never the project itself — it's whether you can name specific decisions, tradeoffs, failures, and

chunking/embedding choices fit it, what retrieval strategy you used and why (dense-only vs. hybrid, re-

precision/recall — not just 'it worked well'), and at least one concrete problem you hit and how you
diagnosed and fixed it. Interviewers are listening for whether you actually made and can defend
specific design decisions, versus describing a generic RAG tutorial.

This question is testing your debugging process as much as the final fix. Strong answers name the
specific symptom (e.g., 'answers were technically correct but missing context' or 'retrieval kept
surfacing near-duplicate chunks'), how you traced it back to a root cause (was it chunk size, embedding
model mismatch, missing hybrid search, absence of re-ranking), the specific change you made, and

access to, and how did you constrain its behavior?

for most closely — the specific guardrails you put in place: permission boundaries, human-confirmation
steps for risky actions, loop/iteration limits, and how you handled tool failures. A project description
that never mentions safety/failure handling reads as a demo, not production experience.

know it was ready, and how did you monitor it after launch?
Walk through both offline and online evaluation: what your pre-launch eval set looked like and how you
built it (real examples vs. synthetic, how you handled edge cases), which metrics you tracked and why
they were the right ones for this specific feature, and what you monitored post-launch (user feedback
signals, automated quality sampling, cost/latency). Bonus points for mentioning a case where
evaluation caught a real regression before or after launch — it signals the evaluation process was
actually load-bearing, not a formality.

Behavioral & Judgment Questions
GenAI engineering roles are judged as much on judgment and communication as on technical depth.
These questions probe how you think about failure, tradeoffs, and cross-functional work — prepare a
real, specific story for each, not a generic answer.
BEHAVIORAL
Tell me about a time an AI system you built produced a wrong or harmful output.
What did you do?
Use a structured (STAR) answer. Interviewers want to see: how you detected the failure
(monitoring/eval, not luck), your root-cause process (did you separate retrieval vs. generation failure,
was it a prompt issue vs. a data issue), the concrete fix you shipped, and what you changed
structurally (a new eval case, a guardrail, a monitoring alert) so the same class of failure doesn't
silently recur.
BEHAVIORAL
How do you decide when an LLM-based solution is the wrong tool for a problem?
Strong answers mention: tasks needing deterministic, auditable, 100%-reliable outputs (financial
calculations, exact rule-based decisions) are often better served by traditional code/rules; tasks where
a simpler heuristic or classical ML model achieves comparable accuracy at a fraction of the
cost/latency; and tasks where hallucination risk is unacceptable and can't be sufficiently mitigated with
grounding. Show judgment, not LLM-maximalism.
BEHAVIORAL
Walk me through how you'd estimate the cost of running a GenAI feature at
scale before building it.
Estimate expected requests/day, average input+output tokens per request (including any RAG context
or few-shot examples), multiply by the target model's per-token pricing, add embedding/vector-DB
costs if RAG is involved, and stress-test the estimate against worst-case scenarios (long conversations,
large retrieved context). Mention that this estimate should directly inform model-size/routing decisions,
not be an afterthought post-launch.
BEHAVIORAL
How do you stay current in such a fast-moving field?
Be specific and genuine rather than generic — name concrete practices: following key research
labs/papers, running small hands-on experiments with new techniques rather than only reading about
them, participating in relevant communities, and critically evaluating new tools/frameworks against
your own production experience rather than adopting hype uncritically.
